World.title: Taylor pitches $22.5b worth of tax cuts, vows to ‘put Australians first’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalFederal budget Taylor pitches $22.5b worth of tax cuts, vows to ‘put Australians first’ Paul Sakkal Updated May 14, 2026 — 7:50pm ,first published 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese personally insisted on protecting existing negative gearing investors, a change critics say will entrench asset owners’ wealth, as the opposition pledges a $22 billion “tax back guarantee” for voters. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor upped the ante on his campaign against “mass migration” in his budget reply speech that sought to pitch bigger personal tax cuts than Labor and differentiate the Coalition from One Nation after its crushing loss in the Farrer byelection. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor reacts as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks during question time in parliament. Alex Ellinghausen The opposition’s questions on the provisions for landlords, including many cabinet ministers, to keep negatively gearing properties they already own sparked furore in parliament on Thursday. Albanese, dubbed Pinocchio by the Coalition for breaking promises, was forced to withdraw his own comments after calling a backbencher a “moron” in a brawl over his property holdings.



Related Article Federal budget Budget fallout: Next tax war will be over rival income tax cuts A day earlier, Albanese warned Taylor in a one-on-one conversation on the floor of parliament that personal and family arrangements should be off limits and Labor could flip the script to Taylor’s trusts and wealth. It set off a heated argument between the pair when the opposition returned to the line of questioning. In Thursday’s question time, Albanese brushed off questions about whether Labor would consider an inheritance tax and warned Taylor that he was on borrowed time, saying: “Clock’s ticking.” That barb came hours before Taylor’s budget reply speech in which the opposition leader promised to peg the lowest two tax brackets to inflation from 2028, delivering $250 for an average taxpayer in the first year, then $1000 by year four. The plan would cost $22.5 billion over four years, the opposition said. It’s not clear how the opposition will fund the tax cut, given Taylor confirmed he would aim to repeal Labor’s $100 billion tax hikes on investors and trust holders.



Indexation was endorsed by Labor luminary Bill Kelty in an interview with this masthead on Thursday before Taylor’s proposal was made public. Kelty said Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ $250 per year Working Australians Tax Offset announced in Tuesday’s budget was “small”. Nevertheless, Kelty welcomed Labor’s policy as a positive step that opened the door to “real reform” to fix the “fundamental problem for the tax system, which is that it’s not indexed for working people”. Tony Pasin shouts across the chamber for Anthony Albanese to withdraw a comment calling him a “moron”. Dominic Lorrimer Chalmers has rejected indexation, favouring an expansion of the tax offset introduced in Tuesday’s budget. Labor and Treasury weighed options on negative gearing that would have been less generous to existing owners, according to government sources familiar with policy development. But despite the mixed views, Albanese was adamant that changes would not affect the approximately 50 per cent of property investors who already deduct rental losses from income.



Albanese said in question time: “Every one of those police or teachers, fire brigade people, whoever they are, can keep their existing arrangements in place.” He added that the current tax system was “screwing over young Australians”. Albanese and his ministers have been buoyed by the public reaction to Labor’s reversal of its election pledge not to touch property concessions, which the opposition has called a brazen lie. The prime minister conducted a round of FM radio interviews on Thursday and ministers were surprised at the lack of hostility directed towards him from callers. Labor Party research also shows many voters in favour of the changes, though reactions have been mixed, and entrepreneurs including Seek founder Paul Bassat are leading a campaign against what they describe as a stifling tax policy. In his budget reply speech, Taylor said the prime minister had benefited from negative gearing and was now “locking out young Australians” and “pulling up the ladder of opportunity”. Taylor promised “one of the biggest cuts to migration in history” though he did not nominate a target, pledging to deport 75,000 people who overstay visas in another plank of his hardline immigration plan.



His speech contains more policy announcements than a normal budget reply speech, particularly so early in the term and three months into his leadership, as the new Coalition leader lays big bets on cutting through following the Farrer byelection defeat by One Nation. Shadow ministers were not brought into the loop on most of the changes. “There’s much work the Coalition must do to win your confidence,” Taylor said, according to an advance copy of his speech. “But with the policies I’ve announced tonight – and the vision I’ve outlined – I hope you can begin to believe again.” The opposition, unlikely to win the next election on current polling, is also promising to bank upgrades to tax receipts based on commodity price upgrades. The savings will be funnelled into a “Future Generations Fund”. After Labor announced a permanent $20,000 instant asset write-off for businesses, Taylor said he would offer up to $50,000.



Taylor was blocked by former opposition leader Peter Dutton last term from pursuing a version of his Tax Back Guarantee, designed to ensure income tax brackets rose each year in line with inflation. In his new pledge, after targeting the bulk of voters in the lower and middle tax brackets, the Coalition would apply indexation to higher income earners from 2031. Related Article Federal budget Albanese gambles on support from younger Australians as he dramatically shifts wealth “That will fully protect all taxpayers from inflation,” Taylor said. “This is generational tax reform.” Taylor will also announce that the Coalition would make Australian citizenship a condition of receiving welfare payments. Leading economists Chris Richardson and Saul Eslake said they opposed grandfathering in principle. However, Richardson said it appeared to be the “political cost of getting change accepted”.



Eslake said grandfathering amounted to “privileging people on the basis of birth order”, but noted that the negatively geared properties would eventually phase out over about eight years. The government believed grandfathering was the cleanest approach that avoided changing the goalposts and creating distortions. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: ‘Too little, too late’: Talks fail to solve Magic Round train dispute
World.content:
Rugby league fans will be able to catch trains to Magic Round games this weekend, but should expect disruptions after an eleventh-hour attempt failed to resolve a dispute between Queensland Rail and unions. The two parties are stuck without a deal on Thursday night after another day of talks at the Fair Work Commission. Commuters are set to be crammed in like sardines, with more three-car trains running as Queensland Rail blames the unions. William Davis The unions – most prominently the Rail, Tram and Bus Union – have been taking action as part of their negotiations for new enterprise bargaining agreements, with this week’s services running similar to a Saturday timetable as QR addresses a maintenance backlog. On its Facebook page, the RTBU claimed it had extended an olive branch on Thursday, which had been rejected by the employer.



“In a sign of good faith we offered to QR a proposition to suspend some of our notified industrial action over the impending NRL Magic Round weekend, specifically the ban on special event trains, if they agreed to some sensible and easy to agree to movement,” the statement said. “QR responded by telling us that they would get no benefit from lifting the action and rejected our offer.” Related Article City life Transport and road closure details for the Brisbane Magic Round Queensland Rail rejected that characterisation of the meeting, saying it had been given “a fake offer and an 11th hour bid by the unions to save face after risking Magic Round”. “They have actually rejected our claims to lift all protected industrial action,” a spokesperson said in a statement.



“It was too little, too late – our people have worked tirelessly around their industrial action to mitigate their impacts and run extra services for footy fans.” The rail authority had already promised to run dozens of extra six-car trains despite the action. The union said the talks were starting to make progress, and they still hoped they could secure “six new EAs that work for our members”. One major sticking point for the unions has been Queensland Rail’s insistence they negotiate with unions as a bloc, rather than independently. Last week, the Fair Work Commission said it had cautioned both parties against “using incorrect terminology in the media”, saying that it would only inflame the dispute and mislead the public.



“I discourage the unions from saying they have been ‘locked out’ when describing a s.471(4) notice and equally discourage the use of the word ‘strike’ when referring to a partial work ban,” a statement said. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: ‘This will really hurt’: Council to confiscate belongings from homeless in St Kilda
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘This will really hurt’: Council to confiscate belongings from homeless in St Kilda Cara Waters May 14, 2026 — 7:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Council officers in the City of Port Phillip are preparing to confiscate the personal belongings of the homelessunder new local laws. The council voted last week to allow staff to seize personal possessions of rough sleepers, including bedding, in response to “anti-social behaviour”. Homeless bedding in Fitzroy Street in St Kilda. Chris Hopkins As councils across Melbourne grapple with homelessness, the City of Melbourne was this week criticised over the interactions of its private security force with rough sleepers and Maribyrnong City Council recently voted to end Footscray’s controversial private security patrols. Mayor Alex Makin told The Age that the City of Port Phillip was responding to increased concerns around safety with homeless encampments in St Kilda, prompting particular concern.



“The impact we’re seeking is a safer environment for rough sleepers and for our community,” he said. “This is not about targeting people in the situation of rough sleeping. It is about managing behaviours that are not suitable, behaviours where someone is at risk to themselves or a risk to others.” About 25 people sleep rough each night in Port Phillip, with more in cars, couch-surfing or in crisis accommodation. Related Article City life Surging crime prompts Port Phillip Council to consider fining homeless Makin said possessions would be safely stored in council service centres or with service providers and readily available for collection at no charge. “We easily could have gone down that path of simply outlawing rough sleeping,” Makin said. “This is a nuanced approach that recognises that there are rough sleepers, they need to be protected, and that’s why we’re addressing behaviours.”



A spokesperson for Victoria Police said reform in local laws, underpinned by the Human Rights Charter, was needed to ensure governance, accountability and a coordinated commitment to a therapeutic approach. Crime rates in Port Phillip are higher than the Victorian average. In the year ending June 2025, Port Phillip recorded 10,974 criminal incidents per 100,000 people, compared to the Victorian average of 6,814. Port Phillip Councillor Libby Buckingham stands in a laneway that has become a popular spot for the homeless. Buckingham opposes the new local laws. Joe Armao At the lengthy and emotive council meeting, Elizabeth Martinov said she had lived in St Kilda for 45 years and had been chased and attacked by a rough sleeper outside the local pharmacy and had an encampment of homeless people set up directly in front of her home. “What followed was not just inconvenience, but unsafe and unsanitary conditions, drug use in public, syringes thrown over my fence, human waste and food scraps left to rot,” she said. “People who are homeless need real help, housing, support, services and pathways out of addiction and instability, but allowing encampments to grow unchecked is not helping them, and it is not protecting the wider community.”



A survey conducted by Port Phillip of 708 respondents found 76.1 per cent opposed the proposed law change. Related Article Exclusive

City of Melbourne City of Melbourne told Joel to ‘not be afraid to use force’. Then they fired him However, at the council meeting five councillors voted in favour of enabling the confiscation of possessions and three against. Councillor Libby Buckingham opposed the change and said that rather than making the streets safer, it would add to conflict and further entrench poverty in the area. “Taking a punitive approach further isolates people, and it aggravates a lot of the problems that see them behaving in a certain way,” she said.



Ruth Gordon, homelessness network coordinator at Launch Housing, said residents who supported the confiscation of possessions thought it was going to be a “magic bullet”, but it was unlikely to make much difference. “It’s just going to make things worse for those individuals who get their stuff confiscated, they’re still going to be homeless,” she said. Gordon said there was a systems failure with services for mental health, medical and housing all across Melbourne. “Ten years ago we could have got them into private rental or set them up with a little bit of help,” she said. “Now it’s just really, really tough to get housing for people.” Rory La Roche, a street outreach project worker at sex worker organisation Vixen, said people were “really devastated and scared” about how the changes in Port Phillip would play out.



“If they are removing people’s shelter and warmth, that is all they have to protect themselves from Melbourne winter,” she said. ”If that is being targeted with being removed, even bedding, there’s going to be violations of people’s human rights and really harsh impacts on the many people sleeping rough that have disabilities and chronic health conditions.” La Roche said parallels could be seen with the approaches taken by other councils, including in the City of Melbourne. Related Article Homelessness Northern suburbs churches open to rough sleepers as winter hits “We’re seeing an even more punitive approach happening in the City of Melbourne, with these security forces moving people on, confiscating items and being permitted to use force against unhoused people,” she said. “Life is already so hard on the street, so doing anything to make things harder for this community is, it’s just really brutal.” La Roche pointed to Maribyrnong Council where the community had pushed back against private security in Footscray with punitive approaches to homeless people.



“That’s a really inspiring example of local people coming together in community to band around and act in solidarity with people sleeping rough and people on the streets,” she said. Federal Labor MP Josh Burns said the decision by Port Phillip failed to respect people’s dignity and human rights and did nothing to fix the policy failures that led to homelessness. “It’s actually a counterproductive measure that’s going to hurt the most vulnerable people and not make people safer,” he said. “I just don’t see the logic in it.” Last year the City of Port Phillip proposed fining rough sleepers camping on council land, roads or footpath, but abandoned the plan after concerns that the laws might not meet human rights legislation. World.title: A bursary helped Joseph become a doctor. He fears trust changes will deny others that opportunity
World.content:
Dr Joseph De Zylva didn’t grow up rich. His family, he says, were likely below the poverty line. His school supplies in high school came from a bursary that set him on the path to university, and medicine. “Clearly it was a person from an area of privilege who supported me,” the Northern Territory doctor said. “I’m concerned these changes will mean trust funds will now be offloading that money to the government … and they’ll be unwilling or unable to help kids like me in the future.” Dr Joseph De Zylva said he was worried about the impact the new tax change might have for his family. That is a reference to the federal budget announcement on Tuesday that there would be a 30 per cent minimum tax on a trust’s taxable income from July 2028, replacing the current system where the amount of tax paid is based on the marginal tax rate of the trust’s various beneficiaries. The current system – which remains in place while the government attempts to legislate the changes – allows the beneficiaries of the more than 840,000 family trusts in Australia to split income between parents who may be earning more, and children earning less, reducing their overall tax bill.



Related Article Investing ‘The days of multiple properties are over’: How to invest after the budget About 90 per cent of private trust wealth is held by the wealthiest 10 per cent of households, according to data cited by the government on Tuesday. Treasurer Jim Chalmers branded the government’s planned change as one that would “level the playing field”, better aligning taxes paid on earnings from vehicles such as trusts with taxes on wages. But there are other reasons people use trusts. IQ Accountants partner Kyelie Baxter said many people had come to her concerned about the changes but that there was not yet enough detail about how it would work. “It could affect how people pay their mortgage and how they fund their children’s education,” Baxter said. “Trusts can also be used to handle bankruptcy and divorce, and are often used to plan out succession. They’re a clean way of passing on a business to next generations.”



De Zylva said he was also worried about the impact the changes would have on some of his female relatives. “Being able to access a family trust allows them to have a supported income at an older age, reducing the burden on the aged care pension,” he said. And he said it benefited younger women in his family too, who could access more of their family’s wealth directly. Some forms of trust are exempt from the government’s planned changes, including charitable trusts. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has vowed to repeal Labor’s tax changes, including to family trusts, while shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chalmers were leading the highest taxing government in Australian history. HLB Mann Judd tax consulting partner Peter Bembrick said the latest change came as little surprise but would lead to “a lot more compliance”, hesitation to open trusts, and some people potentially moving their finances towards a company structure rather than a trust.



“Companies are already attractive vehicles,” he said. “But it’s a bit of a ‘wait and see’ situation. People shouldn’t make rash decisions based on the announcement because the start date [for the change] is not immediate.” Related Article Tax deductions Dozens of politicians set to be hit by new tax on trusts Business groups have claimed the new tax on trusts could stifle business investment. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry acting chief executive David Alexander said the new tax would hit family-owned businesses hard at a time when they were already struggling. “Higher taxes on these small and medium-sized businesses will cut their ability to employ, innovate, and invest in the future,” he said. Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black said he was “disappointed” in the decision to introduce the new tax on trusts, and that a huge number of tradespeople relied on trust arrangements.



A spokesperson for the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia said feedback it received suggested the measures were still being worked through by small business owners, accountants and advisers, with many still trying to understand the practical implications and potential unintended consequences of the policy change. World.title: America’s Cup bid the realisation of a 17-year dream for Tom Slingsby
World.content:
SportSailingAmerica's Cup America’s Cup bid the realisation of a 17-year dream for Tom Slingsby Frances Howe May 14, 2026 — 7:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Olympic sailing gold medallist Tom Slingsby first floated the idea of an Australian return to the America’s Cup as a 23-year-old rooming with teammate Glenn Ashby at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In the years since then, the idea has simmered at the back of the Sydney to Hobart and SailGP winner’s mind, nearly coming to the boil after his own America’s Cup win on Team USA’s Oracle in 2013. Tom Slingsby will lead Australia’s return to the America’s Cup. Louise Kennerley “I was actively going out and seeing what I could do, and back then it felt like it was just too big an ask,” he said on Thursday. Slingsby shared his pipe dream with long-time friend and businessman John “Herman” Winning Jr. Over the past decade, the pair, who have known each other for some 30 years, routinely discussed – and dismissed – their chances of challenging the cup. That was until now.



On Thursday, with the silver trophy known as the “Auld Mug” present at the Royal Price Edward Yacht Club in Sydney, Slingsby was announced as head of sailing for the Australian bid return to the 38th America’s Cup next year. Joining him was Beijing Olympics teammate Ashby, who will head up performance and design, as well as chief executive Grant Simmer, who was navigator on the winning 1983 Australia II. “It’s obviously a hugely personal thing for us to always want to represent Australia at the America’s Cup. For my generation of sailing, we always felt like it’s been a pipe dream,” Slingsby said. Tash Bryant will be the first Australian woman to compete in the America’s Cup’s main division. Ian Walton for SailGP “For me, it’s been quite a long wait, and Glen Ashby, we’ve both been talking about this since we were roommates getting ready for the 2008 Olympics, saying ‘One day we’ll get our shot’.” A shot at actually winning the cup remains a long way off, given the full Australian team is yet to be decided and the yacht – a hand-me-down from Team New Zealand – won’t travel to Australia before being shipped to Italy for racing next year.



Related Article America's Cup ‘Australia taking on the world’: America’s Cup hero welcomes new trophy tilt The Australian team will first compete in the Louis Vuitton Cup, the challenger selection series that will determine who earns the right to face the defending champion Kiwis in the America’s Cup match in July 2027, in Naples, Italy. But Slingsby is hopeful this challenge won’t be a one-off. “It’s an uphill battle,” he said. “We won’t be on the water sailing until next year, whereas other teams have been training for a couple of years. To say that we’re going to win the cup, it’s a big statement. I think we’re hopefully going to be very competitive this America’s Cup. “I think it’ll be very successful if we’re going out there winning races and feeling like we can win any race that we head into, but I think this is a longer-term project and I think we’re setting the foundation now for long-term future for Australia being a force to be reckoned with in the cup.”



Joining Slingsby on board will be Tash Bryant, the first Australian woman to compete in the America’s Cup outside the Youth and Women’s division. The 38th America’s Cup will be the first edition in which each crew is mandated to include at least one woman. Bryant has spent the last four years as the strategist on Slingsby’s championship-winning SailGP team. Related Article America's Cup ‘A completely different world’: Why the modern America’s Cup is unrecognisable “We spoke about the first time I remember watching the America’s Cup and watching the guys race out on the water, it was incredible,” Bryant said. “I loved watching it, but I definitely didn’t see a future or a career path for me … It’s just incredible to see what’s happening now.” It will be up to Simmer to pick the rest of the Australian team, although many of the country’s best sailors are already contracted to other America’s Cup teams. Slingsby is hopeful they’ll be able to poach them back in years to come. “You look at the defender, team New Zealand. They’ve got an Australian skipper and an Australian trimmer and flight controller right next to them,” Slingsby said. “Who knows, maybe they’ll come back next time.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Labor tries to change a housing nightmare into a dream
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Labor tries to change a housing nightmare into a dream May 14, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Photo: Cathy Wilcox Despite Angus Taylor’s protestations, the Great Australian Dream has always been to simply own your own home, not to become a tycoon with a property portfolio (heavily subsidised by taxation perks) outbidding first home buyers and pushing up prices. Largely thanks to John Howard’s capital gains tax changes in 1999, unaffordable housing has become the great Australian nightmare, with prices increasing twice as fast as wages growth. Housing, in effect, has been transformed from a social need into a profitable commodity for speculative investors, at the expense of fairness to younger Australians. Labor’s bold taxation changes to property investment are necessary and long overdue.

Rob Dalton, Torquay Let us hope that fairness prevails

Shaun Carney (Comment, 14/5) provides a clear-eyed overview of the political landscape as the government’s tinkering with property taxes is revealed. Both sides of politics have broken election pledges when they perceived an opportunity to make changes that are good for the country. The difference between Labor’s current changes and John Howard’s decision to impose a GST, after previously ruling it out, is that the treasurer is proposing to take something away from people to which they believe they are entitled. It’s human nature to hold on to what we have rather than relinquish it for the greater good. Let’s hope that fairness prevails and the combined wisdom of the parliament allows the new laws to pass, with vigorous debate and appropriate amendments if necessary.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris Demonising investors is a bit rich

Your correspondent (Letters, 13/5) encourages a move from stamp duty to land tax on residential property, and has a stab at the investors ″⁣sitting on empty land″⁣. However, that would be a poor investment with all property subject to land tax already, unless it is a home (principal residence). The unlucky investor might also be paying local government rates and be accumulating a liability for capital gains tax, along with other holding costs, and the inability to negatively gear if the investment doesn’t generate income. Some property owners used to be farmers who had their land rezoned and couldn’t afford to keep farming, so had to sell up, for a windfall profit. With property and investment there is a labyrinth of complexity and perverse opportunity which has been created by government intervention in the market: subsequent governments can unravel it, but demonising those who invested according to prevailing rules is a bit rich.

Clyde Ronan, Yarrawonga



Look to super as a prime performer

Current property investors are not impacted by the changes to negative gearing rules. Hence there should be no reason to increase rents nor sell investment properties. However, an investment property sold will be bought by either another investor (big deal) or a former renter becoming a home owner (hooray). The reduction in rental stock supplied is offset by the reduction in the demand for rental properties. Furthermore, who would be interested in an investment property (cleaning and maintenance worries and cashflow pressures) when we have a world class, tax effective, consistently good performer, in our superannuation industry. I have had investment properties before and they are, by and large, not worth the effort and the unpredictability.

Tim Habben, Hawthorn Renters should not be the forgotten people

The Coalition talks about aspirational Australians. It seems to favour those who aspire to owning their own home and a rental property against people who want to buy their own home.

I guess it depends on what you aspire to. In my view, the government could do much more for the latter but I guess this is the best that they will get.

John Rome, Mt Lawley, WA THE FORUM Uncertain identity

What is Australia becoming? The headline, ″⁣Jewish care homes hire guards″⁣ (14/5), should send a shiver up every Australian spine. People of the Jewish faith not only have armed guards at children’s school gates, they now have to resort to them to guard the elderly.

Are these measures part of the Australian values that politicians love to talk about? As an atheist, I thought Australia was a country that was free to practise or not practise whatever religion you cared to follow. Should we subject other religions in Australia to harassment based on the actions of their country of origin?

Peter Roche, Carlton The promises trap

Political parties are in a no-win position when it comes to so-called “broken promises”. In the lead-up to every election, the media continually asks “gotcha” questions like “will you rule something in or out?” If the party sensibly replies, “We are not ruling anything in or out”, the media report they won’t rule it out so they and the other party run with that throughout the campaign. So because the party has no way of knowing what the situation will be like during the whole term of the next government, they rule it out.

We want governments to make decisions in the best interests of all of us, and when they need to change based on changing circumstances, and providing they provide a valid explanation, we should support that decision.

David Parker, Geelong West



Useless exercise

Tit for tatting about which politician or political party broke an election promise is a useless pastime as both major parties are guilty. At election time the media love to box politicians into a corner on what they will or won’t do, particularly in regards taxation because they know what a fraught subject that is. A politician will be disinclined to tell the truth or even leave the door ajar because of the consequences. Just ask Bill Shorten.

Phil Labrum, Trentham End the secrecy

Like your correspondent, I keep wishing for more courage and transparency from the Albanese government (Letters, 14/5). Hiding the response to the gambling inquiry behind the curtain of the budget lock-up, when Australia’s political reporters were preoccupied, was poor form. So, too, is Labor’s habit of approving climate-wrecking coal and gas projects late on Friday afternoons.

The Centre for Public Integrity has reported that freedom of information transparency has declined under Labor, with only

25 per cent of requests fully granted. A government that hides its decisions can’t expect confidence in them. For the sake of our democracy, the secrecy needs to end. It’s time to open the books.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Working 9 to 5

Peter Hartcher wrote that ″⁣China’s youth find it hard to get jobs, and when they do, they find a ’996 culture‴⁣⁣ (Opinion, 12/5), working 9 to 9, 6 days a week. Perhaps there’s a simple solution to both problems: 955.

John Shortridge, Blackburn Migrants not the problem

The Coalition and One Nation have linked their immigration policies to Australia’s housing needs, but there seems to be little understanding by them of the housing construction workforce.

I invite Angus Taylor to come to Doncaster and walk the streets with me. There is a lot of housing renewal in Doncaster, demolishing 1960s and 1970s houses and rebuilding them, either as multiple townhouses or (unwanted) huge mansions. I invite Taylor to look at the ethnicity of many tradesmen.

They are largely immigrants, and without them we would have a very limited housing construction industry. Migrants are not the problem; they are the solution, particularly if that involves increasing supply.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Power of music

Last Wednesday night, I sang, danced and cried to Split Enz at Rod Laver Arena. At times, I was transported back to the ’70s when I first heard them. But they are no heritage act. From Tim Finn’s soaring vocals, to Neil’s guitar playing, Eddie sublime on keyboard and Noel’s magnificent graphics and spoonplaying, this was a band still relevant, still bringing a huge crowd to our feet, still so wonderful. This is the power of music. Thank you, Enz.

Carolyn Brand, Point Lonsdale



Labour forces

We have travelled throughout Australia in recent years. Virtually every roadhouse is staffed by overseas people and every town has signs for help wanted. There are shortages of labour across most industries, and yet we hear calls to limit migration purportedly because of housing shortages. Migrants are needed not just for their labour but for the boost they give to aggregate demand. To deny this is dogwhistle politics and opportunism at best and racism at worst.

Stephen Dinham, Metung Reform for all

Listening and reflecting on the various responses from journalists, commentators, the business lobby and a variety of interest groups, one can despair at the lack of reality offered when more is demanded of services the community needs. The call by the federal opposition to restore the tax benefits and breaks to those who have funds to invest is a dismal reflection on policy formulation and conversation of ideas at different levels of society.

Strategies to share the wealth of this nation among all generations is an urgent policy goal and should be acknowledged as a social and ethical issue for the nation.

Headlines that set the agenda for the federal election as “rival tax policies” favouring one group at the cost of the others that is two years away is irresponsible.

Columnist Ross Gittins is one exception with his practical advice and comment not disguised in jargon and statistics.

Constructive and a shared vision for just tax reform that will benefit all Australians should be the goal to enhance the wellbeing of all Australians providing housing, health, education and income.

Ray Cleary, Camberwell No incentives to save

Over the next two years, the government appears set to draw more revenue from those who have worked hard, invested prudently, and planned for a secure retirement. Then, just ahead of the election, it will offer tax breaks to a younger demographic.

Removing the private health insurance rebate for older Australians is likely to have a ripple effect, placing additional strain on an already pressured public hospital system.

At the same time, there seems to be little appetite to address the advantages enjoyed by those benefiting from negative gearing. Is this reluctance influenced by the fact that many politicians themselves hold multiple investment properties – or is that simply a cynical view?

Taken together, these measures risk undermining confidence and reducing the incentive to save for the future.

Trish Young, Hampton Soccer it is

Why can’t some people get used to the fact that in Australia the round ball game is called soccer. “Football” here is played on a large oval with an ovoid ball. Regional variations are common in English and should be accepted. We don’t go to England and tell them their ″⁣pavements″⁣ should be called ″⁣footpaths″⁣;

or go to America and tell them their car ″⁣trunk″⁣ should be called a ″⁣boot″⁣.

What makes it more galling is that Australian football was first codified in 1858, whereas soccer (or as they call it in England, ″⁣association football″⁣) wasn’t codified until 1863, so in a sense we have a prior claim. And a version of our football may have been played here by First Nations people for thousands of years, before England was even a thing.

So let’s be clear: in Australia, we call the round ball game “soccer”, and that’s OK. Live with it.

Ian Robinson, Cowes Different times

When considering the hysteria about “broken electoral promises″⁣, we should remember two things. First, all politicians make electoral promises and many are broken.

Second, the quote attributed to legendary economist John Maynard Keynes: ″⁣When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?″⁣

Circumstances have changed dramatically since the last batch of election promises were made, and it would be the height of irresponsibility and stupidity to be driven by promises made in very different times.

Bob Malseed, Hawthorn East



Here’s to Green Guide

As a former producer and manager at the ABC, Thursday was always Green Guide Day –

a chance to hear from audiences through letters, and the critic’s reviews.

The Green Guide covered emerging media technologies, which mattered to early adopters like me, and practical insights including Terry Lane’s camera and video reviews. Even the s for computer parts were worth reading!

While the Green Guide needed to evolve in response to the web and declining advertising revenue, it remains a must read every week.

Congratulations to Debi Enker and the team.

As far as I am concerned, Thursday will always be Green Guide Day.

Here’s to another 50 years!

Andrew Williamson, Carnegie Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Promises, promises . . . and the Liberal Party will be attaching the broken promise label on Labor while forgetting that its former leader John Howard promised no GST.

Bruce Dudon, Woodend



″⁣Assault on aspiration″⁣, says Angus Taylor. What about the aspirations of young people seeking a home? Negative gearing and capital gains discounts have ensured that their entry to the market is definitely under assault.

John Taylor, Cobram It would be educational for all if the National Press Club in Canberra invited Pauline Hanson to provide One Nation’s reply to the budget. A great variety of media will be able to question her.

Julie Miller, Northcote Orange is the new ignorant.

Russell Kidd, Carnegie It is interesting that many are saying the negative gearing and capital gains changes are ″⁣too little too late″⁣. I wonder if they voted for or against bigger changes when Bill Shorten proposed them in 2016.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn Furthermore

Australians who view US President Donald Trump unfavourably will be breathing a sigh of relief that the proposed Trump Tower on the Gold Coast has come to grief.

Eric Palm, Gympie, Qld



Your correspondent (Letters, 14/5) obviously doesn’t pay land tax or seen the amount of houses for sale on the Mornington and Bellarine peninsulas. Land tax is the killer.

Ian Anderson, Ascot Vale Clive Palmer persists with his campaign for a 25 per cent tax on gas exports. I doubt there are many matters on which he and I would agree but that is certainly one.

John Walsh, Watsonia Finally

And with 80 per cent of the players around the ball, (Letters 14/5) modern football reminds me of Coolaroo Rovers Under 10s, circa 1968.

Peter McGill, Lancefield

World.title: Taylor pitches $22.5b worth of tax cuts, vows to ‘put Australians first’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalFederal budget Taylor pitches $22.5b worth of tax cuts, vows to ‘put Australians first’ Paul Sakkal Updated May 14, 2026 — 7:50pm ,first published 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese personally insisted on protecting existing negative gearing investors, a change critics say will entrench asset owners’ wealth, as the opposition pledges a $22 billion “tax back guarantee” for voters. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor upped the ante on his campaign against “mass migration” in his budget reply speech that sought to pitch bigger personal tax cuts than Labor and differentiate the Coalition from One Nation after its crushing loss in the Farrer byelection. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor reacts as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks during question time in parliament. Alex Ellinghausen The opposition’s questions on the provisions for landlords, including many cabinet ministers, to keep negatively gearing properties they already own sparked furore in parliament on Thursday. Albanese, dubbed Pinocchio by the Coalition for breaking promises, was forced to withdraw his own comments after calling a backbencher a “moron” in a brawl over his property holdings.



Related Article Federal budget Budget fallout: Next tax war will be over rival income tax cuts A day earlier, Albanese warned Taylor in a one-on-one conversation on the floor of parliament that personal and family arrangements should be off limits and Labor could flip the script to Taylor’s trusts and wealth. It set off a heated argument between the pair when the opposition returned to the line of questioning. In Thursday’s question time, Albanese brushed off questions about whether Labor would consider an inheritance tax and warned Taylor that he was on borrowed time, saying: “Clock’s ticking.” That barb came hours before Taylor’s budget reply speech in which the opposition leader promised to peg the lowest two tax brackets to inflation from 2028, delivering $250 for an average taxpayer in the first year, then $1000 by year four. The plan would cost $22.5 billion over four years, the opposition said. It’s not clear how the opposition will fund the tax cut, given Taylor confirmed he would aim to repeal Labor’s $100 billion tax hikes on investors and trust holders.



Indexation was endorsed by Labor luminary Bill Kelty in an interview with this masthead on Thursday before Taylor’s proposal was made public. Kelty said Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ $250 per year Working Australians Tax Offset announced in Tuesday’s budget was “small”. Nevertheless, Kelty welcomed Labor’s policy as a positive step that opened the door to “real reform” to fix the “fundamental problem for the tax system, which is that it’s not indexed for working people”. Tony Pasin shouts across the chamber for Anthony Albanese to withdraw a comment calling him a “moron”. Dominic Lorrimer Chalmers has rejected indexation, favouring an expansion of the tax offset introduced in Tuesday’s budget. Labor and Treasury weighed options on negative gearing that would have been less generous to existing owners, according to government sources familiar with policy development. But despite the mixed views, Albanese was adamant that changes would not affect the approximately 50 per cent of property investors who already deduct rental losses from income.



Albanese said in question time: “Every one of those police or teachers, fire brigade people, whoever they are, can keep their existing arrangements in place.” He added that the current tax system was “screwing over young Australians”. Albanese and his ministers have been buoyed by the public reaction to Labor’s reversal of its election pledge not to touch property concessions, which the opposition has called a brazen lie. The prime minister conducted a round of FM radio interviews on Thursday and ministers were surprised at the lack of hostility directed towards him from callers. Labor Party research also shows many voters in favour of the changes, though reactions have been mixed, and entrepreneurs including Seek founder Paul Bassat are leading a campaign against what they describe as a stifling tax policy. In his budget reply speech, Taylor said the prime minister had benefited from negative gearing and was now “locking out young Australians” and “pulling up the ladder of opportunity”. Taylor promised “one of the biggest cuts to migration in history” though he did not nominate a target, pledging to deport 75,000 people who overstay visas in another plank of his hardline immigration plan.



His speech contains more policy announcements than a normal budget reply speech, particularly so early in the term and three months into his leadership, as the new Coalition leader lays big bets on cutting through following the Farrer byelection defeat by One Nation. Shadow ministers were not brought into the loop on most of the changes. “There’s much work the Coalition must do to win your confidence,” Taylor said, according to an advance copy of his speech. “But with the policies I’ve announced tonight – and the vision I’ve outlined – I hope you can begin to believe again.” The opposition, unlikely to win the next election on current polling, is also promising to bank upgrades to tax receipts based on commodity price upgrades. The savings will be funnelled into a “Future Generations Fund”. After Labor announced a permanent $20,000 instant asset write-off for businesses, Taylor said he would offer up to $50,000.



Taylor was blocked by former opposition leader Peter Dutton last term from pursuing a version of his Tax Back Guarantee, designed to ensure income tax brackets rose each year in line with inflation. In his new pledge, after targeting the bulk of voters in the lower and middle tax brackets, the Coalition would apply indexation to higher income earners from 2031. Related Article Federal budget Albanese gambles on support from younger Australians as he dramatically shifts wealth “That will fully protect all taxpayers from inflation,” Taylor said. “This is generational tax reform.” Taylor will also announce that the Coalition would make Australian citizenship a condition of receiving welfare payments. Leading economists Chris Richardson and Saul Eslake said they opposed grandfathering in principle. However, Richardson said it appeared to be the “political cost of getting change accepted”.



Eslake said grandfathering amounted to “privileging people on the basis of birth order”, but noted that the negatively geared properties would eventually phase out over about eight years. The government believed grandfathering was the cleanest approach that avoided changing the goalposts and creating distortions. World.title: ‘Too little, too late’: Talks fail to solve Magic Round train dispute
World.content:
Rugby league fans will be able to catch trains to Magic Round games this weekend, but should expect disruptions after an eleventh-hour attempt failed to resolve a dispute between Queensland Rail and unions. The two parties are stuck without a deal on Thursday night after another day of talks at the Fair Work Commission. Commuters are set to be crammed in like sardines, with more three-car trains running as Queensland Rail blames the unions. William Davis The unions – most prominently the Rail, Tram and Bus Union – have been taking action as part of their negotiations for new enterprise bargaining agreements, with this week’s services running similar to a Saturday timetable as QR addresses a maintenance backlog. On its Facebook page, the RTBU claimed it had extended an olive branch on Thursday, which had been rejected by the employer.



“In a sign of good faith we offered to QR a proposition to suspend some of our notified industrial action over the impending NRL Magic Round weekend, specifically the ban on special event trains, if they agreed to some sensible and easy to agree to movement,” the statement said. “QR responded by telling us that they would get no benefit from lifting the action and rejected our offer.” Related Article City life Transport and road closure details for the Brisbane Magic Round Queensland Rail rejected that characterisation of the meeting, saying it had been given “a fake offer and an 11th hour bid by the unions to save face after risking Magic Round”. “They have actually rejected our claims to lift all protected industrial action,” a spokesperson said in a statement.



“It was too little, too late – our people have worked tirelessly around their industrial action to mitigate their impacts and run extra services for footy fans.” The rail authority had already promised to run dozens of extra six-car trains despite the action. The union said the talks were starting to make progress, and they still hoped they could secure “six new EAs that work for our members”. One major sticking point for the unions has been Queensland Rail’s insistence they negotiate with unions as a bloc, rather than independently. Last week, the Fair Work Commission said it had cautioned both parties against “using incorrect terminology in the media”, saying that it would only inflame the dispute and mislead the public.



“I discourage the unions from saying they have been ‘locked out’ when describing a s.471(4) notice and equally discourage the use of the word ‘strike’ when referring to a partial work ban,” a statement said. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: ‘This will really hurt’: Council to confiscate belongings from homeless in St Kilda
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘This will really hurt’: Council to confiscate belongings from homeless in St Kilda Cara Waters May 14, 2026 — 7:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Council officers in the City of Port Phillip are preparing to confiscate the personal belongings of the homelessunder new local laws. The council voted last week to allow staff to seize personal possessions of rough sleepers, including bedding, in response to “anti-social behaviour”. Homeless bedding in Fitzroy Street in St Kilda. Chris Hopkins As councils across Melbourne grapple with homelessness, the City of Melbourne was this week criticised over the interactions of its private security force with rough sleepers and Maribyrnong City Council recently voted to end Footscray’s controversial private security patrols. Mayor Alex Makin told The Age that the City of Port Phillip was responding to increased concerns around safety with homeless encampments in St Kilda, prompting particular concern.



“The impact we’re seeking is a safer environment for rough sleepers and for our community,” he said. “This is not about targeting people in the situation of rough sleeping. It is about managing behaviours that are not suitable, behaviours where someone is at risk to themselves or a risk to others.” About 25 people sleep rough each night in Port Phillip, with more in cars, couch-surfing or in crisis accommodation. Related Article City life Surging crime prompts Port Phillip Council to consider fining homeless Makin said possessions would be safely stored in council service centres or with service providers and readily available for collection at no charge. “We easily could have gone down that path of simply outlawing rough sleeping,” Makin said. “This is a nuanced approach that recognises that there are rough sleepers, they need to be protected, and that’s why we’re addressing behaviours.”



A spokesperson for Victoria Police said reform in local laws, underpinned by the Human Rights Charter, was needed to ensure governance, accountability and a coordinated commitment to a therapeutic approach. Crime rates in Port Phillip are higher than the Victorian average. In the year ending June 2025, Port Phillip recorded 10,974 criminal incidents per 100,000 people, compared to the Victorian average of 6,814. Port Phillip Councillor Libby Buckingham stands in a laneway that has become a popular spot for the homeless. Buckingham opposes the new local laws. Joe Armao At the lengthy and emotive council meeting, Elizabeth Martinov said she had lived in St Kilda for 45 years and had been chased and attacked by a rough sleeper outside the local pharmacy and had an encampment of homeless people set up directly in front of her home. “What followed was not just inconvenience, but unsafe and unsanitary conditions, drug use in public, syringes thrown over my fence, human waste and food scraps left to rot,” she said. “People who are homeless need real help, housing, support, services and pathways out of addiction and instability, but allowing encampments to grow unchecked is not helping them, and it is not protecting the wider community.”



A survey conducted by Port Phillip of 708 respondents found 76.1 per cent opposed the proposed law change. Related Article Exclusive

City of Melbourne City of Melbourne told Joel to ‘not be afraid to use force’. Then they fired him However, at the council meeting five councillors voted in favour of enabling the confiscation of possessions and three against. Councillor Libby Buckingham opposed the change and said that rather than making the streets safer, it would add to conflict and further entrench poverty in the area. “Taking a punitive approach further isolates people, and it aggravates a lot of the problems that see them behaving in a certain way,” she said.



Ruth Gordon, homelessness network coordinator at Launch Housing, said residents who supported the confiscation of possessions thought it was going to be a “magic bullet”, but it was unlikely to make much difference. “It’s just going to make things worse for those individuals who get their stuff confiscated, they’re still going to be homeless,” she said. Gordon said there was a systems failure with services for mental health, medical and housing all across Melbourne. “Ten years ago we could have got them into private rental or set them up with a little bit of help,” she said. “Now it’s just really, really tough to get housing for people.” Rory La Roche, a street outreach project worker at sex worker organisation Vixen, said people were “really devastated and scared” about how the changes in Port Phillip would play out.



“If they are removing people’s shelter and warmth, that is all they have to protect themselves from Melbourne winter,” she said. ”If that is being targeted with being removed, even bedding, there’s going to be violations of people’s human rights and really harsh impacts on the many people sleeping rough that have disabilities and chronic health conditions.” La Roche said parallels could be seen with the approaches taken by other councils, including in the City of Melbourne. Related Article Homelessness Northern suburbs churches open to rough sleepers as winter hits “We’re seeing an even more punitive approach happening in the City of Melbourne, with these security forces moving people on, confiscating items and being permitted to use force against unhoused people,” she said. “Life is already so hard on the street, so doing anything to make things harder for this community is, it’s just really brutal.” La Roche pointed to Maribyrnong Council where the community had pushed back against private security in Footscray with punitive approaches to homeless people.



“That’s a really inspiring example of local people coming together in community to band around and act in solidarity with people sleeping rough and people on the streets,” she said. Federal Labor MP Josh Burns said the decision by Port Phillip failed to respect people’s dignity and human rights and did nothing to fix the policy failures that led to homelessness. “It’s actually a counterproductive measure that’s going to hurt the most vulnerable people and not make people safer,” he said. “I just don’t see the logic in it.” Last year the City of Port Phillip proposed fining rough sleepers camping on council land, roads or footpath, but abandoned the plan after concerns that the laws might not meet human rights legislation. World.title: A bursary helped Joseph become a doctor. He fears trust changes will deny others that opportunity
World.content:
Dr Joseph De Zylva didn’t grow up rich. His family, he says, were likely below the poverty line. His school supplies in high school came from a bursary that set him on the path to university, and medicine. “Clearly it was a person from an area of privilege who supported me,” the Northern Territory doctor said. “I’m concerned these changes will mean trust funds will now be offloading that money to the government … and they’ll be unwilling or unable to help kids like me in the future.” Dr Joseph De Zylva said he was worried about the impact the new tax change might have for his family. That is a reference to the federal budget announcement on Tuesday that there would be a 30 per cent minimum tax on a trust’s taxable income from July 2028, replacing the current system where the amount of tax paid is based on the marginal tax rate of the trust’s various beneficiaries. The current system – which remains in place while the government attempts to legislate the changes – allows the beneficiaries of the more than 840,000 family trusts in Australia to split income between parents who may be earning more, and children earning less, reducing their overall tax bill.



Related Article Investing ‘The days of multiple properties are over’: How to invest after the budget About 90 per cent of private trust wealth is held by the wealthiest 10 per cent of households, according to data cited by the government on Tuesday. Treasurer Jim Chalmers branded the government’s planned change as one that would “level the playing field”, better aligning taxes paid on earnings from vehicles such as trusts with taxes on wages. But there are other reasons people use trusts. IQ Accountants partner Kyelie Baxter said many people had come to her concerned about the changes but that there was not yet enough detail about how it would work. “It could affect how people pay their mortgage and how they fund their children’s education,” Baxter said. “Trusts can also be used to handle bankruptcy and divorce, and are often used to plan out succession. They’re a clean way of passing on a business to next generations.”



De Zylva said he was also worried about the impact the changes would have on some of his female relatives. “Being able to access a family trust allows them to have a supported income at an older age, reducing the burden on the aged care pension,” he said. And he said it benefited younger women in his family too, who could access more of their family’s wealth directly. Some forms of trust are exempt from the government’s planned changes, including charitable trusts. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has vowed to repeal Labor’s tax changes, including to family trusts, while shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chalmers were leading the highest taxing government in Australian history. HLB Mann Judd tax consulting partner Peter Bembrick said the latest change came as little surprise but would lead to “a lot more compliance”, hesitation to open trusts, and some people potentially moving their finances towards a company structure rather than a trust.



“Companies are already attractive vehicles,” he said. “But it’s a bit of a ‘wait and see’ situation. People shouldn’t make rash decisions based on the announcement because the start date [for the change] is not immediate.” Related Article Tax deductions Dozens of politicians set to be hit by new tax on trusts Business groups have claimed the new tax on trusts could stifle business investment. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry acting chief executive David Alexander said the new tax would hit family-owned businesses hard at a time when they were already struggling. “Higher taxes on these small and medium-sized businesses will cut their ability to employ, innovate, and invest in the future,” he said. Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black said he was “disappointed” in the decision to introduce the new tax on trusts, and that a huge number of tradespeople relied on trust arrangements.



A spokesperson for the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia said feedback it received suggested the measures were still being worked through by small business owners, accountants and advisers, with many still trying to understand the practical implications and potential unintended consequences of the policy change. World.title: NRL: NZ Warriors star Luke Metcalf signs with St George-Illawarra Dragons, but still has role to play
World.content:
Photo: Blake Armstrong/Photosport

NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster insists halfback Luke Metcalf still has a role to play, as the Auckland club chases its first NRL championship.

Unable to displace in-form Tanah Boyd or Chanel Harris-Tavita in the starting line-up, and apparently intent on playing halfback, not five-eighth, in the long term, Metcalf was given permission to speak to other clubs about his future beyond this season.

On Thursday night, he informed the Warriors he had reached an agreement with another club, signing a three-year deal with St George-Illawarra Dragons.

Metcalf earlier attended training, but has not been selected for either first grade or the reserves this weekend, while he explores his future contract options.

During the summer, Metcalf signed a two-year contract extension until the end of 2028.

"It's dumb for business to name people, to play people, to put them in harm's way, until they've got their future sorted," Webster explained. "The moment he does that, we'll have him available for selection either in NSW Cup or NRL."

Now that seems resolved, Metcalf will likely see out the rest of the season at Mt Smart, where he still has a role in the squad.

"One-hundred percent," Webster assured. "A week in rugby league is a long time, and whoever is playing the best and deserves the opportunity will take it.

"We're certainly not going to change that and he could have a big part to play."

Boyd is just an injury - or State of Origin selection - away from missing time for the Warriors, with Metcalf still the next best No.7 option on the roster.

"We're really blessed that we've got Te Maire Martin, we've got Luke Metcalf and all our young halves," Webster said. "Luke Hanson has played this year and Jett Cleary is tracking well, so we've got a lot of players that could fill in.

"Luke wants to be here for the rest of this year at least and, if he's playing well and buying in, he's certainly available for selection."

Webster was adamant there was no suggestion Metcalf would leave before the end of this campaign, but watching the saga play out in public had been frustrating.

"To see it in the media before we knew a lot about it... people were talking about it before we knew, but the way Luke has handled it with me, particularly in the last three days, has been awesome. I'm really proud of him.

"You always want to get ahead of it and be the first to know.

Photo: Blake Armstrong/Photosport

"He wants to make sure he can explore his future, but at the same time, I know he's very grateful to this club and loves this club. His training's been good, the way he's been around the boys, but rugby league players are ambitious.

"His future's here right now for as long as he wants to be here. It's not an argument or a blow-up or anything like that.

"I haven't seen him train poorly, it's just unfortunate that form from other players has been exceptional, there's been some injuries to Luke himself and he now wants to explore where he wants to go from here."

Webster warns fans not to judge Metcalf too harshly.

"To ask if I'm disappointed they don't want to hang around and fight, I don't know what they're going through," he said. "I don't know how much it's hurting them and I don't know how much strain it's putting on them.

"I honestly think Warriors fans are awesome like that. There will always be at every club one or two idiots that will get it wrong.

"Just treat him with respect. We still love him here and have a lot of time for him, so I hope all the fans feel the same."

Warriors skipper Mitch Barnett has put Metcalf's wellbeing ahead of any disruption the fallout may have caused.

"End of the day, in rugby league, people come and go," he said. "It's a business and for us, as a team, we have to check in with Luke to make sure he's alright - we don't get involved in the other stuff.

"All we expect here is for people to rip in on the training field and deliver on the weekends, and buy into the team culture. He's been doing that, so that's as far as I go.

"For Luke, it's his business and not something I'm willing to comment on. We just check in on the welfare of the human being.

"We've got a game to prepare for. Yes, we care about the individual... we're all around him."

Barnett himself has been granted an early exit from his Warriors contract to return across the Tasman next year on compassionate grounds, signing with Brisbane Broncos.
